1	# Product Definition: AI Fire Sprinkler Inspection App
2	
3	## Problem Statement
4	
5	Fire sprinkler inspections are mandated annually for every commercial building under NFPA 25. Today, 50,000+ inspectors manually identify sprinkler head types, visually check for deficiencies (paint overspray, corrosion, obstruction, wrong temperature rating), take photos for documentation, and then spend 30-60 minutes per site writing up NFPA 25-compliant reports. This process has three failure modes:
6	
7	1. **Missed deficiencies** -- Human fatigue in buildings with 500+ sprinkler heads leads to overlooked corrosion, paint contamination, and obstruction issues. A single missed deficiency can void insurance coverage and create liability.
8	2. **Report generation bottleneck** -- Inspectors spend 40-50% of their time on paperwork, not inspection. Report writing is the #1 complaint in industry surveys.
9	3. **Inconsistent quality** -- Junior inspectors lack the pattern recognition of veterans. A 2-year tech may not recognize a temperature rating mismatch in a high-heat environment. There is no scalable way to transfer expert knowledge.
10	
11	**Confidence: HIGH** -- These pain points are well-documented in fire protection trade publications and confirmed by the existence of Inspect Point ($28M raised to solve the workflow/paperwork problem alone).
12	
13	## Product Scope v1 (MVP)
14	
15	### Core Features (Must-Have for Launch)
16	
17	| Feature | Description | Technical Approach |
18	|---------|-------------|-------------------|
19	| **Sprinkler Head Identification** | Point iPad camera at sprinkler head; AI identifies type (pendent, upright, sidewall, concealed, ESFR), orientation, and manufacturer | CNN image classifier, ~50 classes |
20	| **Deficiency Detection** | AI flags: paint/coating on head, visible corrosion, physical obstruction within 18" clearance, leaking, missing escutcheon, wrong temperature rating for environment | Object detection + anomaly detection models |
21	| **Temperature Rating Verification** | Cross-reference detected head color code against room classification (kitchen, boiler room, attic, standard) | Color classification + building zone metadata |
22	| **NFPA 25 Report Generation** | Auto-generate inspection report with findings, photos, code references, pass/fail per device, summary for building owner | Template engine + findings → code violation mapping |
23	| **Offline Capability** | Full functionality without internet (model runs on-device); sync when connected | CoreML/ONNX on-device inference, background sync |
24	
25	### Explicitly Out of Scope for v1
26	
27	- Fire alarm system inspection
28	- Fire extinguisher inspection
29	- Scheduling/dispatch (integrate with Inspect Point or ServiceTrade instead)
30	- Invoicing/payments
31	- Customer portal
32	- Pipe inspection (standpipes, risers)
33	- Sprinkler system design/hydraulic calculations
34	
35	## User Workflow
36	
37	```
38	1. Inspector arrives at site → Opens app → Selects building from list (or creates new)
39	2. App loads building floor plan (if uploaded) or starts fresh inspection
40	3. Inspector navigates to first sprinkler zone
41	4. Points iPad camera at sprinkler head → AI identifies:
42	   - Head type & model (pendent, upright, etc.)
43	   - Temperature rating (via frame color)
44	   - Any deficiencies (paint, corrosion, obstruction, damage)
45	5. App shows detection overlay:
46	   - Green border = PASS
47	   - Red border + label = DEFICIENCY FOUND (e.g., "Paint contamination detected - NFPA 25 §5.2.1.1.1")
48	6. Inspector confirms or overrides AI finding (one tap)
49	7. App auto-captures photo evidence, tags with location/timestamp/GPS
50	8. Repeat for all heads in zone → move to next zone
51	9. When complete → "Generate Report" button
52	10. App produces NFPA 25-compliant PDF:
53	    - Executive summary (pass/fail count, critical findings)
54	    - Per-device detail with annotated photos
55	    - Code references for each deficiency
56	    - Recommended remediation timeline
57	11. Inspector reviews, signs digitally, sends to building owner + AHJ
58	```
59	
60	**Key UX Principle:** The camera IS the interface. Minimize form-filling. The AI should handle identification and classification; the inspector just confirms/overrides.
61

63	
64	| Tier | Price | Includes | Target |
65	|------|-------|----------|--------|
66	| **Solo Inspector** | $199/mo per seat | Unlimited inspections, AI detection, report generation, 5GB storage | Independent inspectors, 1-3 person shops |
67	| **Team** | $299/mo per seat | Everything in Solo + team management, shared building database, bulk export, API access | 5-20 inspector companies |
68	| **Enterprise** | $399/mo per seat | Everything in Team + SSO, custom report branding, AHJ integration, dedicated support, SLA | 20+ inspector companies, national firms |
69	
70	**Revenue math at $299 avg:**
71	- Year 1: 500 seats = $1.79M ARR
72	- Year 2: 1,500 seats = $5.4M ARR (with expansion into fire alarms)
73	- Year 3: 4,000 seats = $14.4M ARR (multi-inspection-type platform)

87	**Confidence: HIGH** -- Publicly verifiable from funding announcements and press.
88

90	
91	### 4. Joule (Fire Protection Software)
92	
93	| Attribute | Details |
94	|-----------|---------|
95	| **What** | Fire protection-specific software (limited public information) |
96	| **Scale** | Unknown -- website was unresponsive during research |
97	| **AI capability** | Unknown, likely none |

100

105	## Indirect Competitors
106	
107	### Paper/Excel/Manual Process (The Real Competitor)
108	
109	**Market share:** Estimated 40-60% of the 15K fire protection companies still use paper forms or basic digital checklists (Word/Excel). This is the biggest "competitor" -- non-consumption.
110	
111	**Why they haven't switched:** (a) Small shops (2-5 inspectors) don't feel enough pain, (b) cost sensitivity, (c) "it works fine," (d) owner is the inspector and doesn't need AI to know what they're looking at.
112	
113	**How to win them:** Don't try initially. Target tech-forward mid-size shops first. Paper shops convert when their competitors start winning bids with AI-generated reports.
114	
115	### SafetyCulture (iAuditor)
116	
117	- $2B+ valuation, general inspection/audit platform
118	- Configurable for fire protection but has ZERO NFPA-specific intelligence
119	- Risk: If they decide to verticalize into fire protection with AI, they have the scale. No evidence they will -- they're broadening, not deepening.
120	
121	### Fieldwire (Hilti)
122	
123	- Construction jobsite management with general inspection capabilities
124	- "Field Intelligence" AI for general construction
125	- Not fire-specific, owned by hardware company Hilti
126	- Low threat to fire inspection niche
127	
128	## Open Source / DIY Risk
129	
130	**Assessment: LOW**
131	
132	| Factor | Finding |
133	|--------|---------|
134	| GitHub repos for "fire sprinkler inspection" | ZERO |
135	| GitHub repos for "NFPA inspection" | ZERO |
136	| Academic papers on CV for sprinkler deficiency detection | NONE FOUND |
137	| Generic defect detection frameworks | Exist (100-3600 stars) but require massive domain adaptation |
138	| Publicly available sprinkler deficiency training datasets | NONE EXIST |
139	| NFPA 25 compliance logic in open source | NONE (regulatory/proprietary) |
140	
141	**Why DIY won't happen:**
142	1. No training data exists publicly. You cannot train a sprinkler deficiency model without thousands of labeled images of painted heads, corroded heads, obstructed heads, etc.
143	2. NFPA 25 is a purchased standard ($$$). The compliance logic requires expert interpretation, not just rule-following.
144	3. The intersection of "can build ML models" AND "understands fire protection inspection" is approximately zero people in the open source community.
145	
146	**Confidence: HIGH** -- Verified through GitHub search, Google Scholar, and arxiv.
147	
148	## Big Tech Risk
149	
150	**Assessment: LOW**
151	
152	| Company | Relevant Capability | Likelihood of Entering |
153	|---------|--------------------|-----------------------|
154	| Google (Cloud Vision) | Generic object detection/classification | Near-zero. Too small a niche. They build platforms, not vertical apps. |
155	| Microsoft (Azure AI) | Computer vision APIs | Near-zero. Same reasoning as Google. |
156	| Amazon (Rekognition) | Image analysis | Near-zero. AWS builds horizontal tools. |
157	| Apple (CoreML) | On-device ML framework | Zero. They provide the infrastructure, not the app. |
158	| Honeywell | Fire protection equipment + IoT platforms | LOW-MEDIUM. They make sprinkler heads but have poor software track record. Inspection is done by third parties, not manufacturers. |
159	| Johnson Controls | Fire protection systems + building automation | LOW-MEDIUM. Same as Honeywell. |
160	
161	**Key insight:** Big tech makes it EASIER to build this product (APIs, frameworks, cloud infrastructure) but will never build it themselves. The $500M-$1B total addressable market is too small for their attention.
162	
163	The real risk from big tech is that they make it easy for Inspect Point or BuildOps to add vision AI. But those companies have had access to Vision APIs for 3+ years and haven't done it -- suggesting organizational/strategic barriers beyond just technical capability.
164	
165	**Confidence: HIGH** -- Based on known big tech strategy patterns and market size analysis.
166	
167	## Competitive Moat Analysis
168	
169	### What Creates Defensibility
170	
171	1. **Proprietary training data** (STRONGEST MOAT)
172	   - Every inspection generates labeled images
173	   - After 100K inspections, the model sees more sprinkler deficiencies than any human inspector ever will
174	   - This data cannot be purchased or scraped -- it must be collected one inspection at a time
175	   - Network effect: more users → more data → better model → more users
176	
177	2. **NFPA 25 compliance engine**
178	   - Deep regulatory knowledge encoded in software
179	   - Jurisdiction-specific variations (AHJ requirements)
180	   - Updates with each NFPA code cycle (every 3-5 years)
181	   - Takes 6-12 months of domain expert collaboration to build correctly
182	
183	3. **Domain-specific model accuracy**
184	   - Generic vision APIs will never match a purpose-trained model for sprinkler deficiency detection
185	   - The difference between 85% accuracy (generic) and 97% accuracy (specialized) is the difference between "annoying" and "indispensable"
186	
187	4. **Inspector trust/workflow habits**
188	   - Once inspectors trust the AI and build it into their daily routine, switching costs are high
189	   - Building history (what was found last year) creates lock-in
190	
191	### What Does NOT Create Defensibility
192	
193	- The app itself (UI/UX can be copied)
194	- Cloud infrastructure (commodity)
195	- Report templates (easily replicated)
196	- Pricing model (anyone can match)
197	
198	## Final Verdict: CONDITIONAL-GO
199	
200	### GO Conditions
201	
202	1. **Training data access** -- Must secure partnership with 1-2 fire protection contractors willing to provide 1,000+ labeled sprinkler images within first 3 months. Without this, the product cannot achieve sufficient accuracy to be useful.
203	
204	2. **Domain expert** -- Must hire or contract a licensed fire protection engineer (PE) or senior NICET IV certified inspector to validate NFPA 25 compliance logic. Cannot ship without regulatory accuracy.
205	
206	3. **Ship in 6 months** -- The window is open because Inspect Point hasn't moved on vision AI. Every month of delay increases the risk they (or someone else) will. First-mover in AI vision for fire inspection is a 12-18 month advantage.
207	
208	4. **Integration strategy** -- Build as a module that can plug into existing workflow tools (Inspect Point, ServiceTrade), not as a replacement for them. Avoid competing on scheduling/invoicing where they are entrenched.
209	
210	### Why GO (Despite Conditions)
211	
212	- Clear, confirmed gap in the market (no one does AI vision for fire inspection)
213	- Regulatory tailwind (NFPA 25 mandates inspections -- demand is inelastic)
214	- Pure software play (no hardware risk, no manufacturing, no inventory)
215	- Network effects on training data create compounding moat
216	- $200K capital is sufficient for MVP (iOS app + cloud model + 6 months runway)
217	- Revenue model is proven (SaaS per-seat, similar to Inspect Point's model)
218	
219	### Why This Could Fail
220	
221	- Training data cold-start problem (need data to build product, need product to get data)
222	- Market may be too small ($500M TAM ceiling) to attract VC for scaling
223	- Inspect Point could add vision AI within 18 months if they see traction
224	- Fire protection companies are notoriously slow adopters of technology
225	- NFPA domain expertise is scarce and expensive

### Claim A: "AI Vision + Fire-Specific quadrant is EMPTY / zero competition" — **FALSE**

This is the single premise the whole 6.70 stands on (drives Moat 8, Tech Risk 7, the entire
GO verdict). Real market:

| Incumbent | Scale (sourced) | NFPA-25 forms | Photo / deficiency capture | AI branded | Pricing |
